title: Anatomy of a Prompt
objective: After this lesson you will be able to decompose any prompt into its four parts (instruction, context, input, output spec), assign content to system/user/assistant roles correctly, and diagnose vague prompts by naming the missing part.
why: Prompting fails the way SQL fails: not from bad models but from missing clauses. 'Summarize this' fails exactly like SELECT without WHERE — underspecified. Every later lesson (specificity, contracts, few-shots, decomposition) repairs one anatomical part; this lesson names the parts so every repair lands somewhere. It is also the vocabulary the entire agent cluster (LangGraph, CrewAI, RAG, MCP courses) speaks.

blocks.text: Every effective prompt carries four parts. **Instruction**: the verb — what to do ('classify', 'extract', 'draft'). **Context**: the background the model can't guess (role, domain, audience, constraints). **Input**: the data to work on (ticket text, product row, conversation). **Output spec**: the shape of the answer (JSON keys, length, tone, language). Missing any one, the model invents it — and invented context is where bad outputs come from.

blocks.code:
INSTRUCTION: Classify the support ticket into one of [billing, shipping, returns].
CONTEXT: You triage for an online shoe store. 'Where is my stuff' is shipping.
INPUT: "My sneakers haven't arrived and it's been two weeks."
OUTPUT: JSON exactly: {"category": "<one label>", "confidence": <0-1>}
blocks.caption: Four labeled parts — vagueness has nowhere to hide

blocks.text: Chat APIs structure messages by **role**. **System**: durable directives (who you are, rules that always hold) — set once per assistant. **User**: the per-turn request + its input data. **Assistant**: prior model turns (few-shot examples live here, Ch.4). The rule of thumb: *stable identity and rules → system; varying task and data → user.* Stuffing per-ticket data into system, or global rules into user turns, both degrade behavior — and leak context budget (Ch.8).

blocks.caption: Assemble by role: stable rules up top, varying data delimited below

blocks.text: Bad outputs diagnose fast with four questions: *What exactly was asked?* (instruction missing → 'summarize this'), *What couldn't it know?* (context missing → wrong domain assumptions), *What was it given?* (input missing/dirty → answers about nothing), *What shape was demanded?* (output spec missing → correct content in unusable form). Most 'model is dumb' complaints resolve to one absent part — add it, re-run, compare.

blocks.title: Assemble the ticket classifier
blocks.note: Run it: expect 2, 'system: 2 rules', 'user has delimiter: true', '["system","user"]'. Then break it deliberately: move the input into system and notice nothing errors — role mistakes fail silently in behavior, which is why the rule of thumb matters.

items: Four parts: instruction (verb), context (unguessable background), input (data), output spec (shape) — vagueness is always a missing part
System holds stable identity/rules; user holds varying task/data; assistant holds example turns
Delimit input from instruction explicitly; diagnose bad outputs by asking which part is absent

exercise.prompt: The returns team complains the bot 'makes up policies'. Their prompt is: 'Handle this return request: <ticket>'. (a) Name the missing parts (two are absent). (b) Rewrite it with all four parts for a shoe store (30-day window, receipt required, final sale excluded). (c) In the playground, assemble it with buildMessages and verify roles + delimiter programmatically.
hints: Absent: context (which policies? window? exclusions?) and output spec (what shape should the answer take — approval + reason? JSON?). Instruction and input exist.
Context: role + the three policy facts. Output spec: JSON with decision/approved (bool), reason (string), next_step. Keep each part labeled.
Assembly check mirrors practice: 2 messages, roles [system, user], delimiter present, policy facts in system, ticket in user.
exercise.why: 'Makes up policies' is missing-context disease: the model filled policy gaps with plausible inventions. Stating the actual policy in system converts invention into application — the single highest-leverage prompt fix there is.

quiz.q: 'Summarize this: <report>' returns a useless summary. Missing part?
options: Instruction precision + output spec: summarize how (length? bullets? for whom?) — 'summarize' alone underspecifies verb and shape
quiz.explain: Diagnose by part: input exists, but the verb is vague and no shape is demanded. Add length, audience, and format — then compare outputs.

quiz.q: Per-ticket text belongs in which role, and why?
options: User — it varies per turn; system holds stable identity/rules
quiz.explain: Roles allocate by stability: system = durable directives, user = varying task + data. Misplacement wastes budget and weakens rule-following.

quiz.q: Why delimit input from instruction explicitly?
options: So the model can distinguish task language from data language — unmarked boundaries let injected or oddly-phrased data read as new instructions (preview of Ch.6)
quiz.explain: Delimiters are structural, not cosmetic: they mark what is command vs content. Ch.6 shows what attacks the boundary — this lesson builds the habit early.

summary: Instruction, context, input, output spec — four parts, roles by stability, delimiters at boundaries. Diagnose every failure by the missing part.
next: Parts named — now sharpen the verb: concrete instructions beat clever ones. Next: specificity.
